imo-2020-01.title: The circumcentre of $PAB$
imo-2020-01.body:
Let $O$ be the circumcentre of triangle $PAB$. It lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$; we show it lies on both angle bisectors.

**The bisector of $\angle PCB$.** Write $\angle CBP=\alpha$, $\angle BAP=2\alpha$, $\angle BPC=3\alpha$. In triangle $BPC$,
$$\angle BCP=180^\circ-\alpha-3\alpha=180^\circ-4\alpha,$$
and $4\alpha<180^\circ$, so $\angle BAP=2\alpha<90^\circ$. Since the inscribed angle $\angle BAP$ of the circle $(PAB)$ is acute, $O$ lies on the same side of $BP$ as $A$, and the central angle is $\angle BOP=2\angle BAP=4\alpha$.

Because $P$ is inside the convex quadrilateral, the ray $BP$ lies inside $\angle ABC$, so $A$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $BP$. Hence $O$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of $BP$, and
$$\angle BOP+\angle BCP=4\alpha+(180^\circ-4\alpha)=180^\circ,$$
so $B,O,P,C$ are concyclic. In this circle the chords $OB$ and $OP$ are equal (radii of $(PAB)$), so $O$ is the midpoint of the arc $BP$ not containing $C$. Equal chords subtend equal inscribed angles, so $\angle BCO=\angle OCP$: the line $CO$ bisects $\angle PCB$.

**The bisector of $\angle ADP$.** The situation is symmetric with the roles of $A,B$ and $C,D$ swapped: write $\angle PAD=\beta$, $\angle PBA=2\beta$, $\angle DPA=3\beta$. Then $\angle ADP=180^\circ-4\beta$, $\angle ABP=2\beta<90^\circ$, so $\angle AOP=4\beta$ with $O$ on the same side of $AP$ as $B$, i.e. opposite to $D$. Thus $\angle AOP+\angle ADP=180^\circ$, $A,O,P,D$ are concyclic, and from $OA=OP$ the line $DO$ bisects $\angle ADP$.

Hence the two bisectors and the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ all pass through $O$. ∎

imo-2020-02.title: Weighted AM-GM, then expand
imo-2020-02.body:
**Step 1: remove the exponents.** The weights $a,b,c,d$ are positive with sum $1$, so the weighted AM-GM inequality applied to the numbers $a,b,c,d$ gives
$$a^a b^b c^c d^d\le a\cdot a+b\cdot b+c\cdot c+d\cdot d=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2.$$
So it suffices to prove
$$(a+2b+3c+4d)(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)<1=(a+b+c+d)^3.$$

**Step 2: expand.** The left side is
$$a^3+ab^2+ac^2+ad^2+2a^2b+2b^3+2bc^2+2bd^2+3a^2c+3b^2c+3c^3+3cd^2+4a^2d+4b^2d+4c^2d+4d^3,$$
and the right side is $\sum a^3+3\sum_{x\ne y}x^2y+6(abc+abd+acd+bcd)$. Subtracting, the inequality to prove becomes
$$b^3+2c^3+3d^3+a^2d+b^2d+c^2d<2ab^2+2ac^2+2ad^2+a^2b+bc^2+bd^2+6(abc+abd+acd+bcd).$$

**Step 3: compare term by term.** Using $a\ge b\ge c\ge d>0$:
- $2ab^2=ab^2+ab^2\ge b^3+b^2d$,
- $2ac^2\ge 2c^3$ and $2ad^2\ge 2d^3$,
- $a^2b\ge a^2d$, $bc^2\ge c^2d$, $bd^2\ge d^3$.

Adding these gives exactly $2ab^2+2ac^2+2ad^2+a^2b+bc^2+bd^2\ge b^3+2c^3+3d^3+a^2d+b^2d+c^2d$, and the extra term $6(abc+abd+acd+bcd)$ is strictly positive. This proves the strict inequality. ∎

imo-2020-03.title: Pairs and an Eulerian circuit
imo-2020-03.body:
**Reduction.** Split the pebbles into the $2n$ pairs $\{k,\,4n+1-k\}$ for $k=1,\dots,2n$; every pair weighs $4n+1$. We will put each pair entirely into one pile. If each colour ends up with exactly two pebbles in each pile, then each pile has $2n$ pebbles, i.e. $n$ pairs, and both piles weigh $n(4n+1)$. So we only need to assign the pairs to piles so that every colour has exactly two of its pebbles in pile $1$.

**Graph.** Make a multigraph $G$ whose vertices are the $n$ colours, with one edge for each pair, joining the colours of its two pebbles (a loop if both have the same colour). Each colour has four pebbles, so every vertex has degree $4$ (a loop counts $2$). We must colour the edges red (pile $1$) and blue (pile $2$) so that at every vertex exactly two of the four edge-ends are red.

**Colouring.** Take a connected component $H$ of $G$ with $v$ vertices. All degrees are even, so $H$ has an Eulerian circuit, a closed walk using each edge once; it has $\frac{4v}{2}=2v$ edges, an even number. Colour the edges of the circuit alternately red, blue, red, blue, ...; since the length is even, the last edge and the first edge also get different colours.

Every time the circuit passes through a vertex $x$ it arrives along one edge and leaves along the next one; these are consecutive in the cyclic order, so one is red and one is blue. The four edge-ends at $x$ are used by exactly two such passes (a loop at $x$ provides the leaving end of one pass and the arriving end of the next). Hence exactly two of the edge-ends at $x$ are red and two are blue.

Doing this in every component gives the required assignment: put the red pairs in pile $1$ and the blue pairs in pile $2$. ∎

imo-2020-04.title: Components are paths
imo-2020-04.body:
Number the stations $1,2,\dots,n^2$ from bottom to top.

**$k=n^2-n$ is not enough.** Let company $A$ run the cars $i\to i+1$ for every $i$ not divisible by $n$, and company $B$ run the cars $i\to i+n$ for $1\le i\le n^2-n$. Each has $n^2-n$ cars with distinct starts and distinct ends, and higher starts give higher ends. Two stations linked by $A$ lie in the same block $\{jn+1,\dots,jn+n\}$; two stations linked by $B$ are congruent mod $n$. A block contains no two distinct stations congruent mod $n$, so no pair is linked by both. (For smaller $k$, delete cars from this example.)

**$k=n^2-n+1$ suffices.** Consider the cars of $A$ as edges of a graph on the stations. Each station is the start of at most one $A$-car and the end of at most one $A$-car, and every car goes upward, so there are no cycles. Therefore each connected component is a chain $s_1\to s_2\to\dots\to s_m$ of cars going upward, and any two stations in the same component are linked by $A$. A forest with $n^2$ vertices and $k=n^2-n+1$ edges has $n^2-k=n-1$ components. The same holds for $B$.

Since $n^2>(n-1)n$, some $A$-component contains at least $n+1$ stations. These $n+1$ stations lie in only $n-1$ components of $B$, so two of them are in the same $B$-component. Those two stations are linked by both companies.

So $k=n^2-n+1$ always works, while every $k\le n^2-n$ can fail.

**Answer: $k=n^2-n+1$.**

imo-2020-05.title: Largest card and a prime
imo-2020-05.body:
We show that for every $n>1$ the numbers must all be equal.

Suppose not, and take a deck $a_1\ge a_2\ge\dots\ge a_n$ with the property and not all equal. Dividing every number by $d=\gcd(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ divides all arithmetic and geometric means by $d$, so the property is kept; hence we may assume $\gcd(a_1,\dots,a_n)=1$.

**Means are integers.** If $\frac{x+y}{2}=\sqrt[m]{c_1c_2\cdots c_m}$ for card values $x,y,c_i$, then the rational number $r=\frac{x+y}2$ satisfies $r^m=c_1\cdots c_m\in\mathbb Z$, so $r$ is an integer (a rational root of $t^m-N$ is an integer).

**The contradiction.** Since the numbers are not all equal, $a_1\ge 2$; let $p$ be a prime factor of $a_1$. Because the gcd is $1$, some card is not divisible by $p$; let $k$ be the smallest index with $p\nmid a_k$. Then $k\ge2$, $p\mid a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}$ and $a_k<a_1$ (they differ, as $p\mid a_1$ but $p\nmid a_k$).

Apply the property to the pair of cards $a_1,a_k$: $x=\frac{a_1+a_k}{2}$ is an integer and $x^m=a_{i_1}a_{i_2}\cdots a_{i_m}$ for some cards. If $p=2$, then $a_1+a_k$ is odd and $x$ is not an integer, impossible. If $p$ is odd, then $p\nmid a_1+a_k$, so $p\nmid x$, hence $p$ divides none of $a_{i_1},\dots,a_{i_m}$. Thus every $i_j\ge k$, so every $a_{i_j}\le a_k$ and
$$x=\sqrt[m]{a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_m}}\le a_k<\frac{a_1+a_k}{2}=x,$$
a contradiction.

**Answer:** for all $n>1$ the numbers are necessarily equal. ∎

imo-2020-06.title: Projections onto the diameter
imo-2020-06.body:
**Reduction to projections.** For a unit direction $u$, project the points of $S$ onto a line with direction $u$ and sort the projections $t_1\le t_2\le\dots\le t_n$. If some gap $t_{i+1}-t_i=g>0$, the line perpendicular to $u$ through the point $\frac{t_i+t_{i+1}}2$ has points of $S$ on both sides (so it separates $S$) and every point of $S$ is at distance $\ge g/2$ from it. So it suffices to find a direction with a gap $\ge\delta_0:=c_0n^{-1/3}$, where $c_0=(3/256)^{1/3}\approx0.227$; then $c=c_0/2$ works.

Suppose, for contradiction, that **in every direction all gaps are smaller than $\delta:=\delta_0$**. Note $\delta\le c_0<\frac14$.

**The diameter.** Let $A,B\in S$ be at maximal distance $R=AB\ge1$. Put coordinates with $A=(0,0)$, $B=(R,0)$. Every point $P=(x,y)\in S$ has $PA\le R$ and $PB\le R$. From $PB\le R$: $(R-x)^2+y^2\le R^2$, so $x\ge0$; from $PA\le R$, $x\le R$. So all projections onto the $x$-axis lie in $[0,R]$, with $0$ and $R$ attained. With $n-1$ gaps each $<\delta$, we get
$$R<(n-1)\delta<n\delta.$$

**Many points near $A$.** Let $T$ be the set of points of $S$ with $0\le x\le\frac12$, and $m=|T|$. Sort the $x$-coordinates: $0=x_1\le\dots\le x_m\le\frac12<x_{m+1}$ (the point $B$ has $x=R\ge1$, so $x_{m+1}$ exists). Then $x_m\le(m-1)\delta$ and $x_m>x_{m+1}-\delta>\frac12-\delta$, so $(m-1)\delta>\frac12-\delta$, i.e.
$$m>\frac{1}{2\delta}.$$

**But they are spread out vertically.** For $P\in T$, $y^2\le R^2-(R-x)^2\le R^2-(R-\tfrac12)^2=R-\tfrac14<R$, so all of $T$ lies in the rectangle $0\le x\le\frac12$, $|y|<\sqrt R$. Two points of $T$ are at distance $\ge1$ but their $x$-coordinates differ by at most $\frac12$, so their $y$-coordinates differ by at least $\sqrt{1-\frac14}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Hence the $m$ values of $y$ span at least $(m-1)\frac{\sqrt3}2$, while they lie in an interval of length $<2\sqrt R<2\sqrt{n\delta}$:
$$\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\Big(\frac1{2\delta}-1\Big)<\frac{\sqrt3}{2}(m-1)<2\sqrt{n\delta}.$$

**Contradiction.** As $\delta<\frac14$, $\frac1{2\delta}-1>\frac1{4\delta}$, so $\frac{\sqrt3}{8\delta}<2\sqrt{n\delta}$, i.e. $\delta^{3/2}>\frac{\sqrt3}{16\sqrt n}$, i.e. $\delta^3>\frac{3}{256\,n}$, i.e. $\delta>c_0n^{-1/3}=\delta_0$. This contradicts $\delta=\delta_0$.

So some direction has a gap of at least $c_0n^{-1/3}$, and the corresponding perpendicular line separates $S$ with every point at distance at least $\frac{c_0}{2}n^{-1/3}$. Thus $c=\frac12(3/256)^{1/3}$ works. ∎
